newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: SOCCER-SWISS FOOTBALL CLUBS LOOK TO BOURSE - PAPER.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-SWISS FOOTBALL CLUBS LOOK TO BOURSE - PAPER.

text.p: Swiss football clubs may in future compete with other European teams in a new arena -- public share markets -- according to an article published in a Swiss newspaper on Sunday.

"Since Saturday, the groundwork has been laid here for clubs to be transformed into public share companies," the SonntagsZeitung said, adding such a move would hopefully allow the clubs to gain new sponsors and investors.
Swiss news agency SDA reported that the Swiss Football Assocation SFV had agreed at a meeting on Saturday to accept clubs set up as publicly-listed companies in the National League.

European football, known in the U.S. as soccer, is no stranger to share markets in Britain where Tottenham Hotspur became the first club to seek a listing in 1983. Other teams followed, including Manchester United Plc.
Some British football teams may even be considering cross-shareholdings in continental European teams.
Outside Britain, at least three teams in Italy and some in other countries as well are said to be talking about possible flotations.

In Switzerland, Zurich's Grasshopper team, and Geneva's Servette have set up companies with a share capital structure, but they are not publicly listed. In Servette's case, the move was tied to allowing French pay television channel Canal Plus to take a 52 percent stake in the club.

However, the SonntagsZeitung added that the Swiss clubs may have a harder time raising capital through bourse listings, noting that match attendence and merchandising revenues here tend to be small compared with those of the British clubs.
